THE BIG PICTURE

Follow the workload.
Find the bottleneck.

Modern AI depends on more than a model. It depends on moving data, executing tensor operations, managing memory, and coordinating processors.

Across two consecutive blocks, you’ll connect these layers through cost models, implementation, and measurement. Staff provide a small language model and reference components; you build selected systems components and explain why they scale.

01 Predict→02 Build→03 Measure
THE DATA BLOCKD1 — D3

From raw text
to a training dataset.

Collect Wikipedia, process it with Spark, then deduplicate, tokenize, and shard it. Study the cost of storage, query execution, and moving data.

Christopher JermaineWeeks 2–7 · Two lectures each week*
Python · Spark · SQL · BPE
THE TRAINING BLOCKT1 — T3

From one GPU
to parallel execution.

Inspect GPU and framework execution, write a small kernel, build communication benchmarks, and reason about data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism.

Yuke WangWeeks 8–13 · Two lectures each week*
PyTorch · JAX · Triton · NCCL

*Weeks 1 and 14 are taught jointly. University closures shorten Weeks 2 and 5.

LEARN BY BUILDING

Six assignments.
A connected system.

Start small. Check correctness.
Then measure at scale.

Each assignment is 7% of your grade. Checkpoint: 20% · Final submission: 80%. The final submission balances correctness (~50%), performance (~20%), and analysis (~30%).

THE CAPSTONE / 13%

Ask a systems question.
Make the evidence speak.

Work in pairs on two controlled experiments using a fixed baseline. Predict the outcome with a cost model, then explain your measurements or traces. A well-supported negative result can earn full credit.

Data systems

Partitioning, joins, shuffles, caching, or data loading. Keep the dataset contents and model fixed.

Training systems

Kernels, compilation, communication, or parallel layouts. Keep model and data fixed; control batch size and precision.

Spec released Week 7Final due May 4

START WHERE YOU ARE

Math and ML background.
Systems curiosity.

Designed for juniors in AI, CS, math, or statistics who are stronger in math and ML than in systems programming. GPU programming, PyTorch, JAX, architecture, and cluster experience are introduced in the course.

Proposed prerequisites

COMP 345 + linear algebra: CMOR 302, CMOR 303, MATH 221, MATH 354, or MATH 355. Python at the level of COMP 182.

The syllabus proposes a prerequisite change; it lists current catalog requirements as COMP 215, 222, and 345.
BEFORE JAN 11

A four-hour head start.

A self-paced primer covers Python, NumPy, the terminal, and git. A short self-check reviews tensor shapes, the chain rule, and gradient-based optimization.

  • Complete the ungraded primer
  • Take the math and ML self-check
  • Activate your cluster account

Materials and account instructions on Canvas.

      Exams test reasoning. Practice exams are provided; you may bring one page of notes. Concept checks allow unlimited attempts and are graded for completion.

      Late work & outages +

      Five slip days per semester, at most two per submission. Reference outputs are released 48 hours after each deadline; no submissions are accepted after that. No slip days on the capstone. Accommodations and outages are handled separately. Cluster outages near a deadline move the deadline.

      Collaboration & AI tools +

      Discuss ideas freely; write your own code and analysis. Provided code and reference outputs are allowed. Don’t share or view others’ code. Capstone partners may share capstone code; individual assignments stay independent until their deadlines.

      AI may explain concepts, read documentation, and help debug. It may not write the parts each handout assigns to you, including selected Spark jobs, kernel and measurement code, collective logic, or gradient synchronization. Cite AI use, including prompts.

      Code check-offs +

      After D3 and T3, complete a ten-minute individual code walkthrough with staff. Each handout publishes the questions, criteria, and grade weight.

      Help, access & shared resources +

      If you fall behind, start the next stage from a reference output. Attend recitation or office hours for tools and concepts. If you miss a checkpoint, a TA will contact you.

      Register with the Disability Resource Center and speak with an instructor early for accommodations. The Rice Honor Code applies. Test at small scale and release resources when finished; idle jobs count against your allocation. Every graded run fits a guaranteed per-student allocation.
